summary:
The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by an Order in Council. Military service is likewise the responsibility of the United Kingdom rather than of the territory.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that guarantee has been in force since 2010.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. The Island Council approved the ordinance unanimously on 1 April 2015, Governor Jonathan Sinclair signed it on 5 May 2015, and it was published on 13 May 2015. The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn, so a visitor or resident entering such a partnership abroad can have it recognised locally.

Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.

The population is roughly 50 residents, and none of them is known to be in a same-sex relationship. A visitor should expect a community of that size in which no local same-sex partnership is publicly visible, alongside statutory protections that are written in formal terms and rarely tested in practice.
tangentialFactors:
The territory's protections sit within a single legal jurisdiction: there are no provincial or municipal variants of the non-discrimination guarantee and no sub-national divergence in how marriage or adoption rules are applied.

The 2010 constitutional guarantee is framed around sexual orientation only as the sources state it. Whether that protection reaches discrimination on grounds of gender identity, and whether any body receives and investigates complaints under it, is not established by the available material.

Because United Kingdom statutes do not extend to the Pitcairn Islands automatically, protections or restrictions familiar from United Kingdom practice, including the 2025 single-sex-services code, are not a reliable guide to what a visitor will encounter here.

Same-sex marriage was enacted locally by the Island Council rather than imposed from outside, which distinguishes the territory's record from jurisdictions where similar rules arrived through external imposition. The territory is routinely indexed within United Kingdom LGBT-rights timelines, a publishing convention that can obscure the fact that local law governs.
localsOnly:
Residents may marry regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity under the Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015, and civil partnerships formed outside the Pitcairn Islands are recognised by the same ordinance.

Adoption is available to married, unmarried and single residents, a scope broader than the married-couple-only rules that operate in many jurisdictions.

The Island Council is the local legislative body that approved the 2015 ordinance unanimously, and the Governor signs and publishes local ordinances; residents seeking to change local law work through that route rather than through the United Kingdom Parliament.

The 2010 Constitution Order gives residents a constitutional guarantee against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in force since 2010.

Defence and external affairs, including military service arrangements, remain with the United Kingdom and are not locally determined.
outOfScopeNotes:
Provisions on legal gender recognition, gender-marker changes on identity or travel documents, and any medical or immigration screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status are not present in the available sources and remain unresolved here.

Whether the Pitcairn Islands have hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, rules governing access to sex-segregated facilities, or restrictions on gender-affirming care is not sourced and should be treated as open rather than as absent.

The available sources are written around sexual-orientation rights. They do not state whether the constitutional non-discrimination guarantee has been interpreted to cover gender identity, and no enforcement mechanism or complaint record is described.

The figure of roughly 50 residents is approximate and undated in the sources, and the statement that no resident is known to be in a same-sex relationship is a source assertion that cannot be independently verified.
